modules.name: Planning and context files
modules.blurb: Separate exploring from building, and give the agent the context it cannot infer.

lessons.title: Explore, plan, then code
goals: Use plan mode to get a reviewable plan before any file changes
Judge when a task is small enough to skip the plan
Write a plan another person could execute: phases, files, verification

facts.claim: Anthropic's best-practices page recommends four phases: explore, plan, implement, commit, and warns that letting Claude jump straight to coding can produce code that solves the wrong problem.
In plan mode Claude reads files and runs shell commands to explore and writes a plan, but does not edit source until the plan is approved.
Plan mode is entered by pressing Shift+Tab until the status bar shows plan mode, by prefixing a prompt with /plan, or by starting with claude --permission-mode plan.

When Claude presents a plan you can approve it with auto mode, approve it while still approving each edit, or keep planning; approving exits plan mode. Ctrl+G opens the plan in your editor to change it first.
Planning adds overhead: for a small, clear change such as a typo or a rename, ask Claude to do it directly. If you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan.

checklist.text: The plan is split into phases that each end in something you can check
It names the files or modules each phase touches
Every phase says how it will be verified, not just what will be built
It names at least one risk or open question and how it will be resolved

lessons.title: CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, and progress files
goals: Put in CLAUDE.md only what the agent cannot infer from the code
Keep context files short, and know what each one costs every session
Keep a progress file that lets a fresh session pick up where the last one stopped

facts.claim: CLAUDE.md files live at the user level (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md), the project level (./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md), and an optional managed policy location set by an organisation.
Claude Code loads CLAUDE.md and CLAUDE.local.md from the working directory and every directory above it and concatenates them; files in subdirectories load on demand when Claude works there.
CLAUDE.md can import other files with @path, but imported files also load at launch, so imports organise a long file without reducing its context cost.
The docs suggest keeping each CLAUDE.md under 200 lines: longer files consume more context and reduce how well Claude follows them.

CLAUDE.md should hold what Claude cannot infer from the code, such as non-default style rules, test commands, repository etiquette, and environment quirks, and leave out what it can work out by reading the code.
Claude Code reads AGENTS.md as project instructions only when there is no CLAUDE.md or CLAUDE.local.md in the working directory or above it.
/init generates a starter CLAUDE.md from the project; when one already exists it suggests improvements instead of overwriting it.

checklist.text: CLAUDE.md holds commands, conventions, and quirks the code does not show
Each CLAUDE.md is under about 200 lines
Nothing is repeated that the agent would learn by reading the code
The progress file ends with the next concrete step and what is blocked

lessons.title: Keep the context window clean
goals: Clear between unrelated tasks and compact with a focus
Know what survives compaction and what does not
Push exploration into a subagent so its reading does not fill your context

facts.claim: /clear resets the context window; the best-practices page recommends it between unrelated tasks.
/compact replaces the conversation with a summary and accepts focus instructions, for example /compact Focus on the API changes.
After compaction the project-root CLAUDE.md is re-injected from disk and nested CLAUDE.md files reload on demand, so durable instructions belong there rather than only in the conversation.
Subagents run in their own context windows and report back only a summary, so their file reading does not fill the main conversation.

checklist.text: Unrelated tasks start fresh, with /clear or a new session, instead of piling up
Compaction happens deliberately, with a focus, not only when the window fills
Broad exploration goes to a subagent instead of the main conversation
Prompts say what done looks like and how to check it

modules.name: Test strength and verification
modules.blurb: Give the agent checks it can run, and make sure those checks test behaviour rather than restate the code.

lessons.title: Give the agent a check it can run
goals: Hand the agent a test, build, or script that decides when it is done
Start a bug fix with a failing test that reproduces it
Tell a test that pins behaviour from one that restates whatever the code returns

facts.claim: The best-practices page notes that Claude stops when the work looks done, and recommends giving it a check it can run, such as tests, a build, a linter, or a script.
For a bug, the best-practices page's example prompt describes the symptom and asks Claude to write a failing test that reproduces the issue, then fix it.
The best-practices page shows putting example test cases in the request and asking Claude to run the tests after implementing.

lessons.title: Tests the agent cannot game
goals: Separate the agent that writes tests from the one that writes code
Have a fresh context grade the work instead of the one that did it
Spot tests written around the current output: snapshot-only asserts, mocks of the unit under test, no edge cases

facts.claim: The best-practices page suggests having one Claude write tests and another write code to pass them.
A verification subagent or a Stop hook can check the work, so the agent doing the work is not the one grading it.
A subagent does not see the parent conversation or the files the parent already read, which is what makes it an independent checker.

modules.name: Reviewing agent output for accuracy and security
modules.blurb: Read an agent's diff the way a careful reviewer would, and set guardrails so the worst mistakes cannot happen.

lessons.title: Catch what the agent got wrong
goals: Find invented APIs, weakened tests, swallowed errors, and scope creep in a diff
Find injection holes, leaked secrets, and missing authorisation
Decide what to check by hand and what to hand to a review subagent

facts.claim: The security page says the user is responsible for reviewing proposed code and commands for safety before approving them.
The Code Review page warns that its AI review may miss bugs, security vulnerabilities, or other issues, and that a review with no findings does not mean the code is error-free or secure.
Under its untrusted-content guidance, the security page recommends avoiding piping untrusted content directly to Claude and verifying proposed changes to critical files.

The best-practices page says a fresh context improves code review because Claude will not be biased toward code it just wrote, and it describes a Writer/Reviewer pattern that uses a second session to review.

The local code-review page says /code-review checks your branch's changes for correctness bugs in a background subagent with its own context window, and works on any plan. Without --fix it asks Claude only for a report; with --fix it also asks Claude to apply the findings, and any edit goes through your permission mode.

The commands reference says /security-review analyzes the changes on your current branch for security vulnerabilities, reviewing the diff against origin's default branch for risks such as injection, auth issues, and data exposure.

lessons.title: Permission modes and guardrails
goals: Choose a permission mode for the task at hand
Write allow and deny rules that are no broader than needed
Use hooks for rules that must hold every time, not prompts

facts.claim: The permission-modes page lists default, acceptEdits, plan, auto, dontAsk, and bypassPermissions as the modes. The config value default is the mode the UI calls Manual, and in it only reads run without a prompt.
The permissions page says rules are evaluated in the order deny, then ask, then allow, and the first match in that order decides the outcome, with rule specificity not changing the order.

The settings page ranks settings from highest to lowest as managed settings, command line (claude --settings), project local (.claude/settings.local.json), shared project (.claude/settings.json), and user (~/.claude/settings.json), and says a key set at a higher level overrides the same key set lower down.
The hooks page says a PreToolUse hook that exits with code 2 blocks the tool call even if it also prints JSON, and that the hook's stderr is the message shown as the reason for the block.
The permission-modes page says deny rules block in every mode, including bypassPermissions, and that allow rules have no effect in bypassPermissions.
The security page says the sandboxed Bash tool isolates bash commands with filesystem and network isolation, reducing permission prompts while maintaining security.

checklist.text: The default permission mode fits how the project is worked on, and bypassPermissions is not the default
Allow rules name specific commands, not whole tools like Bash
Deny rules cover what must never happen, such as reading secrets or pushing to main
A rule that must hold every time is a hook, not a line in CLAUDE.md

modules.name: Skills
modules.blurb: Package a repeatable workflow so the agent loads it only when it is needed.

lessons.title: Write a skill
goals: Turn a workflow you repeat into a SKILL.md
Write a description that makes the skill load at the right moment and no other
Keep the body short and move detail into files the skill reads on demand

facts.claim: The skills page says a personal skill lives at ~/.claude/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md and a project skill lives at .claude/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md, and that enterprise skills take precedence over personal ones, which take precedence over project ones.
The skills page says only the description frontmatter field is recommended, name defaults to the directory name, and all other frontmatter fields are optional.

The skills page says Claude uses the description, plus when_to_use if set, to decide when to load a skill automatically, and advises putting the key use case first because the combined text is cut at 1,536 characters in the listing.
The skills page says a skill's body loads only when it is used, and supporting files referenced from SKILL.md are read on demand, while scripts are executed rather than loaded.
The skills page advises keeping SKILL.md under 500 lines and moving detailed reference material into separate files.
The skills page says setting disable-model-invocation to true prevents Claude from loading the skill automatically, so the skill runs only when the user invokes it with /name.

The skills page documents frontmatter fields including name, description, when_to_use, argument-hint, disable-model-invocation, user-invocable, allowed-tools, model, effort, context, agent, hooks, and paths, and Claude Code ignores fields it does not recognise.

checklist.text: The description says when to use the skill, with the key use case first
The skill does one repeatable job, not a grab bag
SKILL.md stays short and moves detail into files it reads on demand
A skill with side effects can only be run by the user (disable-model-invocation)

modules.name: Loops and automation
modules.blurb: Run the agent without a person at every step, and know when it should stop.

lessons.title: Headless runs and scripts
goals: Run the agent non-interactively for a scripted task
Limit its tools and permissions for unattended runs
Read its output in a form a script can check

facts.claim: The headless page says --output-format accepts text (the default), json, and stream-json, where json returns structured output with the result, session ID, and metadata, and stream-json returns newline-delimited JSON for real-time streaming.

The headless page says to pass --permission-prompts none when nobody can answer permission prompts, such as in a scheduled job, and then anything that would prompt is denied unless a PermissionRequest hook allows it.

The headless page says a -p session shows no workspace trust dialog and no per-server MCP approval prompt, and without --bare it still runs hooks from a project's .claude/settings.json even in a folder you have never trusted.
The headless page says --allowedTools lets Claude use the listed tools without prompting, and a rule like Bash(git diff *) uses prefix matching because of the space before the star.
The CLI reference says --max-turns limits agentic turns in print mode, exits with an error when the limit is reached, and has no limit by default.
The headless page says --continue continues the most recent conversation, and --resume with a session ID continues a specific conversation.

checklist.text: Unattended runs name the tools they may use instead of allowing everything
Nothing waits on a permission prompt nobody will answer
Each run is bounded, for example with --max-turns
A script reads structured output and checks the result, not just the exit code

lessons.title: Loops and stop conditions
goals: Pick a loop's interval from how fast the thing it watches changes
Give every loop a condition that ends it
Know what a loop costs per iteration

facts.claim: The scheduled-tasks page says the /loop bundled skill is the quickest way to run a prompt on repeat while the session stays open.
The scheduled-tasks page says that when /loop is run without an interval, Claude picks a delay of between one minute and one hour after each iteration, based on what it observed.

The scheduled-tasks page says pressing Esc stops a self-paced /loop while it waits for the next iteration by clearing the pending wakeup, and Claude can end the loop itself by calling ScheduleWakeup with stop set to true.
The hooks page says a Stop hook can prevent Claude from stopping and continue the conversation, either by exiting with code 2 or by returning decision block with a reason.

The hooks page says the Stop hook input field stop_hook_active is true when Claude Code is already continuing because of a stop hook, and advises checking it to avoid blocking on a condition that will never resolve.

The hooks page says Claude Code applies a cap of 8 consecutive stop-hook continuations, overriding the next block after eight in a row, that the count resets whenever Claude calls a tool, and that CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_BLOCK_CAP raises the cap.

checklist.text: Every loop or Stop hook has a condition that ends it
A Stop hook checks stop_hook_active so it cannot block forever
A loop's interval matches how fast the thing it watches changes
The cost of each iteration is known and kept small

modules.name: Orchestrators and workers
modules.blurb: Split a task across subagents with the right model, effort, tools, and hand-off for each.

lessons.title: Split work across subagents
goals: Decide which parts of a task to delegate and which to keep
Write a hand-off contract: what each worker gets, may touch, and returns
Run independent workers in parallel and dependent ones in order

facts.claim: Subagents are defined as Markdown files in .claude/agents/ for the current project or ~/.claude/agents/ for every project; the --agents flag, managed settings, and plugins can define them too.
Only name and description are required in a subagent's frontmatter.
Each subagent runs in its own context window with its own system prompt, tool access, and permissions, and does not see the parent's conversation history.
Only a subagent's final summary returns to the main conversation; a background subagent's result arrives later as a notification, and a subagent can be resumed with SendMessage.

checklist.text: Each worker has one job, and the orchestrator keeps the parts that need the whole picture
Each hand-off says what the worker gets, what it may change, and the shape of what it returns
Independent workers run in parallel; dependent ones wait for what they need
Worker output is checked before it is trusted or merged

lessons.title: Pick a model and effort for each worker
goals: Match a worker's model to how hard its job is
Set effort per worker instead of running everything at the maximum
Give each worker only the tools its job needs

facts.claim: A subagent's model field accepts an alias (sonnet, opus, haiku, fable), a full model id, or inherit; when it is omitted Claude Code chooses one.
A subagent's effort field accepts low, medium, high, xhigh, or max, and which levels are available depends on the model.
Subagent frontmatter also documents tools, disallowedTools, permissionMode, maxTurns, skills, mcpServers, hooks, memory, background, isolation, color, and initialPrompt.

checklist.text: Each agent's model matches how hard its job is, with a reason
Effort is set per agent rather than left at the maximum everywhere
Each agent lists only the tools its job needs
Frontmatter uses only documented fields and valid model and effort values

modules.name: Cost and prompt caching
modules.blurb: Know what a session costs, why cached tokens are cheap until they are not, and what breaks the cache.

lessons.title: How prompt caching prices a session
goals: Read a session's cost as cache writes, cache reads, and uncached input
Choose between the five-minute and one-hour cache
Order a prompt so the stable parts come first

facts.claim: Writing to the five-minute cache costs 1.25 times the base input price; writing to the one-hour cache costs 2 times.
Reading from the cache costs 0.1 times the base input price for most models, and less on some of the newest models.
The cache prefix is built in the order tools, system, messages; a change at one level invalidates that level and everything after it, so changing tool definitions invalidates the whole cache.
A request can define up to four cache breakpoints.
Each model has a minimum cacheable prompt length, from a few hundred to a few thousand tokens; shorter prompts are processed without caching and no error is returned.
By default, the prompt cache has a 5-minute lifetime, and the cache is refreshed for no additional cost each time the cached content is used.
The extended 1-hour cache is requested by including ttl with the value 1h in the cache_control definition, alongside type ephemeral.
Cache read tokens are priced at 0.1 times the base input token price, with per-model exceptions of 0.025x on Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1 and 0.05x on Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5.
The lookback window for automatic prefix checking is 20 blocks: the system checks at most 20 positions per breakpoint, counting the breakpoint itself as the first.
When one request mixes TTLs, cache entries with a longer TTL must appear before shorter ones, so a 1-hour cache entry must come before any 5-minute cache entry.
The pricing page lists base input prices per million tokens of $4 for Claude Opus 5.5, $2 for Claude Sonnet 5.5, $3 for Claude Sonnet 4.5, and $1 for Claude Haiku 4.5.
The prompt-caching page lists a minimum cacheable prompt of 512 tokens for Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5, 1,024 tokens for Claude Sonnet 4.5, and 4,096 tokens for Claude Haiku 4.5.

lessons.title: What breaks the cache in Claude Code
goals: Recognise the actions that throw away a warm cache
Plan model and effort switches at natural break points
Decide when compacting is worth the cache it costs

facts.claim: Claude Code manages prompt caching automatically unless it is disabled with environment variables such as DISABLE_PROMPT_CACHING.
In Claude Code, switching models, changing effort on most models, and compacting the conversation invalidate the cache.
Editing CLAUDE.md mid-session does not take effect until /clear, /compact, or a restart.

checklist.text: Instructions that rarely change sit in CLAUDE.md, not in each prompt
Model and effort switches happen at natural break points, not mid-task
Compaction and /clear are used deliberately, with a reason

modules.name: Refactoring with agents
modules.blurb: Know when a refactor pays for itself, and let an agent do it without changing behaviour.

lessons.title: When to refactor, and when not to
goals: Refactor before a change that the current structure makes hard, not for its own sake
Pin behaviour with characterisation tests before the agent touches the code
Keep each refactor step small enough to review and revert

facts.claim: The Refactor code recipe on the Common workflows page includes the tip 'Do refactoring in small, testable increments', and its example asks Claude to keep the same behavior and then run the tests.

The best practices page says to give Claude a check it can run, such as tests, a build, or a screenshot to compare, because Claude stops when the work looks done and 'looks done' is otherwise the only signal available.
Fowler defines refactoring as a change made to the internal structure of software to make it easier to understand and cheaper to modify without changing its observable behavior.
Fowler's Refactoring page says the heart of refactoring is a series of small behavior preserving transformations, and that the system is kept fully working after each refactoring.
Fowler credits Kent Beck with the phrase 'make the change easy, then make the easy change' and writes 'So first I refactor the code into the structure that makes it easy to add the feature.'

modules.name: Working across providers
modules.blurb: When a second model from another provider pays for itself, and how to wire one in.

lessons.title: A second model as reviewer
goals: Use a model from another provider to review a plan or a diff
Weigh what it catches against the cost of a cold context and another vendor seeing the code
Bridge another tool in through MCP, a multi-provider harness, or a gateway

facts.claim: Running claude mcp serve starts Claude Code as a stdio MCP server. The page warns that this server only exposes Claude Code's tools, so the MCP client must implement user confirmation for individual tool calls.

Any gateway that exposes a supported API format works, but Anthropic doesn't endorse, maintain, or audit third-party gateway products, and doesn't support routing Claude Code to non-Claude models through any gateway.
Amazon Bedrock is enabled by setting the environment variable CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK to 1, and the page notes that AWS_REGION is optional when your AWS profile already sets a region.

For a remote MCP server, Claude Code reads credential variables from the environment as empty in the server's url and headers, which keeps a project's .mcp.json or a plugin from sending your Claude Code or cloud provider credentials to a server it names.
MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open-source standard for connecting AI applications to external systems, such as data sources, tools, and workflows.

Codex stores MCP configuration in config.toml, with each server configured in a [mcp_servers.<server-name>] table, and the codex mcp add command can register a server that runs as a local stdio process.

checklist.text: It says when a second model is worth its cost: which changes, not every change
The second model sees only what it needs, and what leaves the machine is a choice
The reviewer's output has a shape the first agent or a person can act on
The bridge (an MCP server, a gateway, or a script) is configured explicitly, with its credentials kept out of the repository
